subject: 메소포타미아의 법전과 분쟁
title: Law codes and disputes in ancient Mesopotamia
content: The law codes inscribed on stone in ancient Mesopotamia are among the earliest legal documents that survive, and they are usually read as the statutes of their kingdoms. Yet the court records from the same centuries rarely cite them, and the judgments they contain often depart from what the codes prescribe. This discrepancy has forced historians to ask what such an inscription was actually for, since it plainly was not consulted in the way a modern statute is. One answer treats the codes as royal display. A ruler who published just decisions advertised that he was the kind of ruler under whom justice was available, and the monument served that claim whether or not any judge ever read it. The prologues support this reading, because they praise the king at length before any provision appears, and they address the gods rather than the courts. On this view the code is a statement about the ruler instead of an instrument for deciding cases. A second answer holds that the codes recorded exemplary judgments which judges already knew, so that citing them was unnecessary. Both readings agree on the important point. Disputes in these ancient cities were settled by local custom, by the testimony of neighbours, and by oath, and the written code stood alongside that practice rather than governing it. Reading the tablets as a legal system therefore imports an arrangement that would not exist for many centuries.

subject: 과학 이론의 미결정성
title: When evidence cannot decide between theories
content: Philosophers of science have long noticed that any body of evidence fits more than one theory, and this point reaches well beyond the seminar room. If two accounts predict the same observations, then no experiment can tell them apart, and our reasons for taking one must come from somewhere other than the data. What that further source could be is the question this problem raises. Some argue that the rival theories in such pairs are usually contrived, built by adding matching tweaks to a real theory so that its predictions survive. Since nobody would propose them on their own, the bare fact that they can be built tells us little about how scientists actually choose. Critics answer that the history of science offers real cases, and that calling a theory contrived requires the very standards whose warrant was in question. A second response accepts the problem and looks to virtues beyond prediction. Simplicity, breadth of explanation, and fit with nearby theories all guide what gets accepted, and scientists appeal to them openly. The difficulty lies in saying why such virtues should track truth rather than mere convenience, since a simpler theory is easier to use whether or not the world is simple. That question stays open, and it is why the topic still bears on how much trust any well-supported theory has earned.

subject: 화약의 전파와 축성의 변화
title: Gunpowder and the rebuilding of fortifications
content: When gunpowder artillery became effective against masonry, the high walls that had protected medieval towns for centuries turned into liabilities, and this reversal is visible in the archaeological record within a few decades. A tall wall presented a large target and collapsed outward when its base was breached, so the very features that had defeated ladders and rams now invited destruction. Builders across the affected regions responded with a design that looked nothing like what it replaced. The new works were low, thick, and faced with earth that absorbed shot rather than shattering under it, and their outline was cut into angled projections so that every stretch of wall could be covered by fire from another. Because these fortifications spread outward rather than upward, they consumed far more land and far more labour than the walls they succeeded. A town that rebuilt on the new pattern committed resources on a scale that only a substantial treasury could sustain. That cost had political consequences the engineers did not intend. Small lordships which had been defensible behind a medieval wall could no longer afford to be, and they were absorbed by powers that could pay for the new works. Historians accordingly connect the spread of gunpowder to the consolidation of larger states, since the technology did not merely change how sieges were conducted but changed who could afford to resist one at all.

subject: 시간의 흐름은 실재하는가
title: Whether time really passes
content: Nothing seems more obvious than the passage of time, and yet philosophers have argued for more than a century that this appearance may mislead us. The dispute concerns whether the present moment has any special status, or whether all times are equally real and our sense of flow is a feature of experience rather than of the world. Both positions have costs, and neither has been able to dismiss the other. Those who hold that passage is real point out that our entire practical life presupposes it. We deliberate about the future and not the past, we regret what is over, and we take the present to be where action happens. A theory on which these distinctions track nothing objective must explain why the illusion is so systematic, and merely calling it an illusion does not do that. Those who deny passage appeal to physics, where the equations treat temporal direction symmetrically and relativity denies that any universal present can be defined. On their account the experience of flow arises because memory accumulates in one direction, so a creature built as we are would feel passage whether or not the world contained it. Critics reply that this explains the feeling by presupposing an asymmetry it was supposed to eliminate, which suggests the argument has not yet reached bottom.

subject: 의식의 주관성 문제
title: The subjectivity of conscious experience
content: A complete physical account of a creature would describe its neurons, its behaviour, and every function its brain performs, and yet philosophers have argued that such an account would leave something out. What it omits is how things seem from the inside, since knowing everything about the mechanism of colour vision seems compatible with never knowing what red looks like. This gap has proved unusually resistant to the strategies that have dissolved other philosophical puzzles. Defenders of the gap press it with thought experiments. A scientist who has learned all the physical facts about vision while confined to a colourless room would still, they argue, learn something new on seeing a ripe tomato, and what she learns cannot be a physical fact because she already had them all. Critics answer that she gains a new way of representing an old fact rather than a new fact, comparing it to recognizing a person one had only read about. That reply is widely discussed and not widely regarded as decisive. What makes the dispute unusual is that both sides accept the same science. The disagreement concerns whether an explanation in functional terms could ever amount to an explanation of experience, and since no experiment bears on that question, it is settled by argument or not at all. Some philosophers conclude that our concepts are simply not built to close this particular distance.

subject: 문명 간 문자 차용의 사례
title: Borrowed scripts among ancient civilizations
content: Writing was invented on its own only a few times in human history, and yet ancient scripts turn up across many regions, because most peoples got writing by borrowing it rather than by making it. This difference matters, since a borrowed script arrives fitted to a language it was not built for, and the changes that follow leave traces a historian can read. Those changes took a few recognizable forms. A script built for a language with simple syllables strains when used for one with dense consonant clusters, so borrowers added signs, gave old ones new duties, or put up with gaps their neighbours would not have accepted. Where the borrowed system wrote consonants only, speakers of languages with many vowels made marks for them, and that step was taken more than once in different places. Because such changes leave dated inscriptions, the order of borrowing can be traced with some confidence. What this pattern shows reaches beyond writing itself. A script travels with the people who use it for accounts, treaties, or scripture, so the map of borrowings records where ancient trade and rule actually reached rather than where chroniclers claimed. Historians therefore treat the awkward fit between a script and a language as evidence, since that awkwardness is just the sign that the system came from elsewhere.

subject: 시민 불복종의 조건
title: The conditions of civil disobedience
content: A citizen who breaks a law she believes unjust raises a moral question that both defenders and critics of the practice take seriously, since a general permission to disobey would dissolve the rule of law while a general prohibition would have condemned reformers we now honour. Political philosophy has therefore tried to state conditions under which such disobedience is justified, and the conditions proposed are more demanding than the popular image suggests. Most accounts require that ordinary channels have been tried and have failed, because a law can be changed by voting where the political system remains open. They also require publicity, since acting openly distinguishes the protester from the ordinary lawbreaker and signals that she accepts the legal order while rejecting one part of it. Willingness to bear the penalty performs the same function, and it is why concealment weakens the moral case rather than strengthening it. A further condition concerns proportion. The wrong protested must be serious enough to justify the disruption caused, and the action must be aimed at that wrong rather than at coercing the public generally. Critics observe that these conditions were formulated with reasonably just societies in mind, and that they offer little to someone facing a system where no channel is open and no penalty is survivable. That objection has not been answered, and it marks the limit of the theory rather than a flaw within it.

subject: 고대 페루의 계단식 경작
title: Terraced farming in the ancient Andes
content: The terraces that cover the slopes of the ancient Andes are usually explained as a way of creating flat ground on steep land, and that explanation is correct as far as it goes. Yet excavation has shown that these structures did considerably more than level a hillside, and the additional functions account for the enormous labour their construction required. Each terrace was built as a layered system rather than as a simple platform. Beneath the soil lay gravel and sand that drained heavy rain away before it could wash the surface off, and the stone facing absorbed heat during the day and released it at night, which extended the growing season at altitudes where frost would otherwise have destroyed a crop. Because these layers had to be assembled by hand and carried up the slope, a single terrace represented seasons of collective work. The agricultural gain therefore cannot be measured by area alone. Fields at different heights on the same slope experienced different temperatures and rainfall, so a community that farmed several levels was spreading its risk across conditions rather than concentrating it, and the ancient records of crop varieties suited to particular elevations support that reading. Historians consequently treat the terraces as an instrument for surviving bad years rather than merely for producing more in good ones.

subject: 익명성과 도덕적 책임
title: Anonymity and moral responsibility
content: People behave differently when they cannot be identified, and this observation is old enough to appear in ancient philosophy, where a ring that conferred invisibility was used to ask whether anyone would remain just without the risk of being seen. Modern conditions have made the question practical rather than hypothetical, since a great deal of conduct now occurs where the actor is effectively unidentifiable. What such conditions reveal is disputed. One view holds that anonymity removes an external restraint while leaving moral character untouched, so that what appears under it was always present and merely suppressed by fear. On this reading the anonymous crowd shows us what people are, and the visible world shows us what they are willing to be seen as. A second view holds that identifiability is partly constitutive of moral agency rather than merely a check upon it, because a person answerable to others has reasons that a person answerable to nobody does not. Both views agree that responsibility is harder to sustain without identification, and they differ about whether that difficulty is a limitation of enforcement or of morality itself. The practical question is unaffected by which is right. Where conduct causes harm and no one can be held to account, the harm persists whatever the explanation, and arrangements that restore some form of answerability address it either way.

subject: 자율과 후견적 개입
title: Autonomy and interference for a person's own good
content: Interfering with someone for her own benefit is among the most contested questions in moral and political philosophy, because two things we value pull against each other. We think that people should direct their own lives, and we also think that allowing avoidable harm is wrong when we could prevent it. Where a person's choice will damage only herself, these commitments deliver opposite verdicts and the conflict cannot be dissolved by appealing to either alone. The classical liberal answer restricts interference to cases where others would be harmed, treating the individual as sovereign over her own affairs. Its defenders argue that nobody is better placed to judge what serves a person than that person, and that granting others the authority to override her invites abuse even when it is well meant. Critics reply that the premise is empirically shaky, since choices are made under pressure, with poor information, and against known patterns of misjudging risk. A middle position distinguishes interference that overrides a decision from interference that improves the conditions under which it is made. Requiring a delay, ensuring that information is present, or altering which option is the default all leave the final choice with the person while addressing the ways it goes wrong. Whether this genuinely respects autonomy or merely disguises the override is the current form of the argument.

subject: 행복과 좋은 삶의 구분
title: Happiness and the good life
content: We often use happiness and a good life interchangeably, and yet philosophers have long argued that the two can come apart in ways that matter. A person may feel contented while being systematically deceived about her circumstances, and most of us judge that something has gone wrong in her life even though nothing has gone wrong in her experience. That judgment is what any account of well-being must explain or explain away. The experiential view holds that well-being consists in how life feels from the inside, so the contented deceived person is genuinely well off and our contrary judgment reflects our own preference for truth rather than a fact about her. Its rival holds that well-being requires that certain things actually obtain, among them real friendships, genuine achievement, and accurate belief, so a life can go badly without ever feeling bad. Each view accounts for some of our judgments and strains against others. A third position lists several goods and denies that they reduce to one another, accepting that well-being has no single measure. This fits ordinary judgment better than either rival, though it gives up the tidiness that made those rivals attractive. What the debate establishes is that a person can be mistaken about how well her own life is going, and that conclusion has consequences for how much weight her reports should carry.

subject: 수학적 대상은 존재하는가
title: Whether numbers exist
content: Mathematical statements appear to be true, and their truth appears to be about something, so philosophers have asked what numbers are if they are anything at all. The question is not idle, because our best physical theories are stated mathematically, and if the entities they quantify over do not exist then the status of those theories becomes obscure. Two broad answers have organized the debate for a century. One holds that mathematical objects exist independently of us, in the way that physical objects do but without location in space or time. This explains why mathematical truths seem discovered rather than invented, and why they hold regardless of what anyone believes. Its difficulty concerns knowledge, since we have no causal contact with such objects and it is unclear how we could learn anything about them. The opposing answer denies that numbers exist and treats mathematical talk as a useful fiction or as a description of structures rather than things. This avoids the epistemological problem entirely, and yet it must explain why a fiction should be indispensable to science, and why some mathematical claims are correct while others are not. Neither answer has prevailed, and the persistence of the disagreement suggests that our ordinary notion of existence was not built to settle cases of this kind.
